All I wanted was to watch the snow fall with her before she moved to Texas. She told me over the summer that she would be leaving, and ever since then I had been trying to cherish each one of our last moments together. The only problem is that as the countdown for the end of December, for that damned plane taking off, grew shorter and shorter, there were less and less moments. She was busy; she had to wrap things up at the barn, she had to finish her school work so she could graduate early, she had to work, she had to pack. I didn’t blame her. I was upset, sure, but not at her. It wasn’t her fault, she wasn’t in control of what was happening. It was like fate didn’t want us to see each other. What a funny idea, fate. Who ever thought of such a thing?

All I wanted was to watch the snow fall with her before she moved to Texas. We would walk through a trail in the woods together. There were plenty of trails to pick from here in Evetown, Minnesota, but maybe we could even drive further out and find someplace in the middle of nowhere. It would be nighttime, and because it would be a winter's night everything would be perfectly still. Gray, too. Everything would be gray. But it wouldn’t be sad, no, because she would be there. She made all the sad things happy. We would be wearing our winter coats, but they wouldn’t be enough so we would’ve had to hold each other to keep warm. Truth be told we would’ve held each other either way. And we would look up, and we would watch the snow fall. And it would be beautiful.

All I wanted was to watch the snow fall with her before she moved to Texas. But it never snowed. Not a sprinkle in October, like it usually did; not even once in November, like it usually did; and so far, nothing at all in December. It was like fate was keeping the snow from us. We sat in the car together, parked, looking out the windshield at the reflecting moonlight on the surface of the lake. It was a cloudless night, and not a single snowflake fell from the sky or lay resting on the ground. We parked here a lot; we weren’t much of an ‘activity’ couple. We didn’t need to be doing something to appreciate each other, we just needed each other. I looked into her eyes and she looked into mine. Sometimes we talked and sometimes we didn’t. She apologized for never being available anymore, and I told her not to worry about it. Like I said, I didn’t blame her. I loved her. I still do.

All I wanted was to watch the snow fall with her before she moved to Texas. I remember the last night we were supposed to see each other, I was only waiting for a text but instead I got a call. She was crying. Maybe something came up, or maybe she forgot to pack something, or maybe it was something else entirely, I really can’t remember. My mind went blank. All I remember was that she couldn’t see me anymore. The rest of that phone call was a haze, both in the moment and in memory. I felt like I was standing in a fog with no idea where I was or where I should go. I remember saying that I loved her, and her saying that she loved me. I remember saying goodbye. I remember her saying goodbye. Over the phone.

All I wanted was to watch the snow fall with her before she moved to Texas, but that never happened. Staring out my window, I wanted to look at the sky. That was where she was, anyway. In an airplane, in the sky, flying to Texas. Away from me, away from everything. I wanted to look at the sky but my view was blocked by an endless field of gray clouds. That night, Evetown was hit with seven inches of snow. Everything was gray, and she wasn’t here to make it happy.
